content: A severe headache that does not go away or gets worse over time, or changes in vision such as blurriness, seeing spots, or flashing lights, are urgent maternal warning signs. These can be symptoms of postpartum preeclampsia, a serious blood pressure condition that requires immediate emergency care.

Heavy postpartum bleeding is a medical emergency. You should seek immediate medical care if you are bleeding heavily, such as soaking through one or more pads in an hour, or passing blood clots the size of an egg or bigger.

Experiencing thoughts of harming yourself or your baby is an urgent medical emergency. Immediate help is required. Reach out to a healthcare provider immediately, call 911, or contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Following a caesarean section, patients should monitor their incision site for signs of infection. Warning signs include worsening localized pain, spreading redness, wound discharge or pus, and a fever. Mild, steadily improving pain is expected during routine recovery.

Breast pain accompanied by a fever, chills, or hard, red, swollen areas on the breast may indicate mastitis, an inflammation or infection of the breast tissue. This often requires medical evaluation and potentially antibiotics. Continued feeding or pumping on the affected side is generally recommended to clear blockages.

Many over-the-counter pain relievers, such as ibuprofen and acetaminophen, are generally considered safe to use while breastfeeding. However, always consult a healthcare provider or the LactMed database before starting new medications, as some drugs can transfer to breast milk and affect the infant.

For non-emergency mental health support, Postpartum Support International (PSI) offers free online support groups, peer mentoring, and a helpline. You can call or text their helpline at 1-800-944-4773 for support and resources. (Note: In an active crisis, call 988 or 911).
